description: One Degree is a team that combines computer science and mechanical engineering to address challenges in lunar exploration, led by Jayan Tasnim. We combine programming, scientific data and engineering perspectives to address challenges in lunar exploration, with the aim of supporting better decisions for future missions.
summary:
One Degree is a terrain-aware planning tool for lunar landing sites and dates. At the lunar south pole, the Sun stays only a few degrees above the horizon, so a single ridge can block sunlight or the view of Earth for hours or even days. Standard sky calculations assume a flat horizon and miss this effect.

Our web app combines NASA LOLA elevation models with JPL Horizons positions of the Sun and Earth. For each site, it traces the real terrain horizon in 720 directions over 150 km and calculates when the Sun and Earth are visible above it. Users can select landing dates from November 2026 to December 2027, compare three candidate south-pole sites, and see how launch delays of one, seven or fourteen days change sunlight and Earth visibility.

We applied the same method to three historical case studies involving the Odysseus, Blue Ghost and Athena landers, comparing our results with their published mission timelines. We also cross-checked terrain elevations and long-term Sun and Earth visibility against NASA LOLA data and relevant visibility products available through LROC QuickMap. The tool helps mission planners, educators and the public understand why landing-site selection and timing matter for lunar surface operations.
details:
What it does
One Degree helps users compare lunar landing sites and landing dates by showing when the Sun and Earth are geometrically visible above the real local terrain. The web app has five sections: Compare Sites & Dates, Local Sky, Timeline, Mission Replay, and Method & Validation.

How it works

  1. Sites: three candidate south-pole sites (Mons Mouton, Malapert Massif, and Nobile Rim 1) and three historical landing sites, with coordinates from LROC QuickMap.
  2. Sun and Earth positions: JPL Horizons, with the observer placed on the lunar surface, gives azimuth, elevation, and apparent disk size. Positions are sampled every hour for planning and every 10 minutes for historical case studies.
  3. Terrain horizon: for 720 directions around each site, rays follow great-circle paths for up to 150 km across NASA LOLA elevation models. The horizon in each direction is the highest apparent terrain angle, using spherical lunar geometry and a 2 m observer height. The 80 m south-pole model is used for the three planning sites and Athena, the 240 m model for Odysseus (near the edge of the 80 m map), and the 474 m global model for Blue Ghost (far from the pole).
  4. Visibility: the app calculates the fraction of the Sun or Earth disk above the terrain horizon and estimates rise and set times between samples.
  5. Scenario comparison: results are computed for every landing day from November 2026 to December 2027, including launch delays of one, seven and fourteen days.

Key findings

  • Over the evaluated year, Mons Mouton has geometric Sun visibility 47.5% of the time and Earth visibility 92.9% of the time.
  • The Malapert Massif target point has Sun visibility 44.1% of the time but no Earth visibility, because a ridge to its north blocks the view.
  • At Mons Mouton, the time with both the Sun and Earth visible in the first 30 days ranges from 194 to 393 hours, depending on the landing date.

Consistency checks

  • Calculated ground heights agree with LROC QuickMap within 0.2–1.4 m at three lander sites.
  • Site rankings for Sun and Earth visibility agree with NASA LOLA long-term visibility maps. At Mons Mouton and Malapert Massif, our share of time with the Sun visible agrees with NASA’s value within 1 percentage point (our one-year period compared with NASA’s 18.6-year average).
  • In the hardest ridge-skimming period tested (Malapert Massif, 1–12 February 2027), the hourly planning calculations detected all eight sunrise and sunset events found with 10-minute sampling, and the estimated event times differed by no more than 13 minutes.

Historical case studies

  • Odysseus: contact ended about 52 hours (±12 h) before the predicted terrain sunset, while the Sun was still fully visible in the model. This is consistent with the lander’s tipped orientation and shows that terrain visibility alone does not explain every mission ending.
  • Blue Ghost: final data arrived 2.9 hours after the predicted terrain sunset; with a flat horizon the figure was 2.3 hours. Firefly reports about five hours. Real terrain moved the prediction 33 minutes closer, but it does not explain the full difference.
  • Athena: the lander came to rest in a crater about 20 m wide, smaller than one pixel of the 80 m map. This case shows a resolution limit of the model.

Benefits and intended impact
Mission planners can quickly see how a site choice or a schedule change affects sunlight availability and Earth visibility. Educators and the public can see why the lunar south pole is difficult: small differences in local terrain can decide whether a lander has a clear view of the Sun or Earth.

Creativity
Most simple approaches show the Sun above a flat horizon or use long-term average maps. One Degree combines real local terrain, JPL Horizons Sun and Earth positions, and day-by-day landing scenarios in one interactive app. It also tests its predictions through historical mission case studies, including a case that exposes the model’s limits.

Factors considered

  • Scientific limits: geometric visibility does not guarantee power generation or an operational communication link.
  • Terrain resolution: features smaller than a map pixel are not represented.
  • Timing accuracy: rise and set times are interpolated estimates, not minute-accurate predictions.
  • Usability: precomputed results keep the app fast and open to anyone without installation.

Tools and software
Python, Streamlit, pandas, NumPy, SciPy, Plotly, Matplotlib, Pillow, rasterio, pyproj, astroquery and Astropy. Development tools: PyCharm and GitHub. Hosting: Streamlit Community Cloud. No physical hardware was used.

Use of Super Intelligence (SI) tools

SI tools (Claude and ChatGPT) were used as learning and productivity aids to save time and allow a wider implementation scope within the hackathon. They helped the team understand technical concepts, explore implementation approaches, draft and debug code, interpret results, and draft and edit written text, including the project page content and the README. The team led the brainstorming, chose the project direction, and proposed several additions. The team made the final technical decisions, reviewed and tested the implementation, and verified the reported results. All project calculations were performed by the project's code using the referenced NASA data sources.
